title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease
summary:
Background and Objective: Bridging kidney MRI with patient-specific computational biomechanics may enable accurate, noninvasive assessment of chronic kidney disease. To develop a finite element method (FEM)-based computational elastography framework for estimating renal biomechanical properties from conventional kidney MRI and to evaluate its ability to differentiate chronic kidney disease (CKD) from healthy controls.
  Methods: Kidney segmentation masks from healthy control and CKD subjects were converted into triangulated surface meshes, and watertight surfaces were tetrahedralized to create volumetric FEM meshes. Kidney tissue was modeled as a nearly incompressible Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic material. Harmonic wave propagation simulations were performed using FEM, followed by Helmholtz-based elastographic inversion to estimate complex shear modulus distributions. Derived biomechanical parameters were used for CKD classification using machine learning models.
  Results: FEM-derived stiffness estimates showed consistency with stiffness ranges previously reported in human renal MRE studies and also showed measurable differences between healthy and CKD groups. Machine learning models trained on FEM-derived features achieved classification performance up to 86.26% cross-validation accuracy with an AUC of 0.92.
  Conclusion: FEM-derived elastographic parameters showed potential for distinguishing CKD from healthy tissue and may provide an alternative for renal biomechanical assessment without dedicated MRE acquisition.

title: Distributed Geometric Optimization and Control of Rigid Differential-Drive Formations from Relative-Position Measurements
summary: Distance based formation control fixes the shape of a robot team but leaves its position and orientation unconstrained. We regulate all three for differential drive robots that have only one absolute position anchor, absolute headings, body frame relative position measurements, and communication with their neighbors. We derive a two layer estimation control scheme directly from optimization. The first half of the result is a set of graph-proximal estimators that reconstruct the centroid, the anchor vector, and the centered coordinates. Exact proximal updates reach consensus in finitely many steps, and a finite number of primal dual iterations leaves a bounded reconstruction error. The controller combines proximal centroid and orientation steps with distance gradient shape regulation, and a finite rotation removes the orientation drift caused by the shape step. A discrete Lyapunov analysis gives local exponential convergence once the estimators have converged. We validate the method in ROS 2 Gazebo and in experiments with five physical robots.

title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
summary: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.

title: State-Feedback Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems
summary: The passivity of a generating station enables network stability to be established from conditions verified locally at each station. For synchronous machines, however, passivity can only be certified under conditions on the operating point, and these conditions fail under heavy loading and weak damping. This paper develops a state-feedback controller that enforces passivity using a storage battery connected at the terminal bus. A bilinear term arising from the product of the rotor-speed and stator-current deviations is treated as a bounded uncertainty, leading to robust positive-real conditions that can be enforced by a state feedback control designed using a single algebraic Riccati equation. The resulting controller guarantees passivity whenever the Riccati equation admits a positive-definite solution, with no separate condition on the operating point. Numerical examples show that existing conditions certify passivity only up to a fraction of the rated current, whereas the proposed state-feedback approach certifies it at the rated operating point of the machine.

title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process
summary: dsp provides a unified state-space framework for modeling nonstationary time series using the Dynamic Shrinkage Process (DSP), a class of global-local shrinkage priors. DSP adaptively regularizes time-varying parameters to shrink noise while preserving abrupt changes and other local structure. The package supports Gaussian and count-data smoothing, changepoint detection, time-varying parameter regression, and volatility estimation, with posterior predictive draws available for missing-value imputation and forecasting. Nonstationary time series often contain periods of relative stability punctuated by abrupt changes in mean or variance. dsp offers a common interface for model specification, posterior computation, summarization, and visualization across models that were previously developed separately in the literature. Core functionality is implemented in C++ via Rcpp for computational efficiency. We describe the underlying models, package design, and the main functions for fitting, summarizing, and plotting posterior results.

title: Towards Comprehensive Mobile Application Testing for User-centric Feature Coverage via Simulating Real-World Users with Personas
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for black-box mobile application testing, where the ultimate goal is the comprehensive coverage of the features users rely on. However, most existing studies focus on Activity Coverage, which measures the proportion of distinct application screens visited during a test session but does not directly measure whether agents actually test the features users care about. To address this, we focus on (1) how to automatically measure whether a testing framework covers the features users care about, and (2) how to design a framework that achieves more comprehensive feature coverage. To answer (1), we introduce the User-Centric Feature Coverage benchmark, which consists of two components: a manually crafted dataset of 3,012 user-centric target features based on real reviews and app descriptions, and an automated evaluation pipeline that translates agent-generated test cases and target features into a shared semantic space, then uses an LLM-as-a-judge to compute coverage. To answer (2), we introduce ECS (Exploration, Critical User Journeys, and Synthetic Reviews). ECS is a framework that explores the application, then uses an LLM to convert exploration traces into Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to bring the semantic meaning of the trace closer to a distinct feature. Each CUJ consists of an LLM-inferred user intent paired with reproducible test steps. ECS then aggregates multiple CUJs using persona-augmented synthetic reviews to capture more complex features, simulating real users who build knowledge of an application across multiple screens before writing a review. ECS achieves 64.1% feature coverage, a 23.8% gain over the state-of-the-art baseline, and covers 72.5% of features in app descriptions, capturing the most prominent features. Our failure analysis shows statelessness and exploration discoverability as main reasons of failures, providing future directions.

title: Few-Shot Beam Selection for Embodied AI via In-Context Learning and Conformal Prediction
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by the 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory Workshop (ISIT 2026 Workshop) on Reliable Machine Learning for Wireless Embodied Intelligence
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications are essential for supporting massive multimodal sensory data exchange in Embodied Artificial Intelligence (EAI) systems. However, fast and reliable beam selection for mmWave communication remains a critical bottleneck due to the prohibitive overhead associated with conventional beam training. Although location-aided beam prediction offers a promising alternative, its performance is often limited by localization errors and the need for extensive training data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework termed In-Context Learning driven Cross-Validation Conformal Prediction (ICL+CVCP) for beam prediction. The proposed framework utilizes the training-free adaptation capability of ICL, enabling effective operation with only a small number of demonstration samples and eliminating the need for large-scale data collection and model fine-tuning. In addition, the CVCP module constructs compact, distribution-free candidate beam sets that provably contain the optimal beam with a user-defined probability. Experimental results confirm that ICL+CVCP consistently satisfies the desired empirical coverage while significantly reducing pilot overhead and computational latency, thereby meeting the stringent reliability and efficiency requirements of EAI applications.

title: Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines with Automatic Model Complexity Inference
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 1 algorithm. Code available at https://github.com/afrakilic/BTTKM
summary: Tensor Network (TN) kernel machines accelerate supervised learning by using low-rank TNs to reduce computation and memory. However, most TN-based methods are deterministic with manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, while the existing Bayesian TN kernel machine is restricted to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (CPD), whose single rank is shared by all modes. We extend this framework to the tensor train (TT) and propose Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), whose hierarchical ARD-type priors on the TT cores infer the TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. Since each TT core is coupled to the others only through its neighbors, its closed-form posterior update requires propagating the contributions of all other cores along the chain. Mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart and a closed-form predictive distribution. A synthetic experiment illustrates that BTT-KM recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.

title: Replay Is a Family of Assertions: Fork-Safety in Event-Sourced Agent Runtimes
comment: 27 pages; executable specification, validation harness, and conformance vectors: https://github.com/yoheinakajima/agent-runtime-laws
summary:
Event-sourced agent runtimes commonly claim deterministic replay, cheap forking, and lineage. These are families of assertions, not one guarantee. A fixed-log fold may be deterministic while reactive settlement remains schedule-sensitive; a recorded oracle result can enable zero-call replay while the original interaction still changed cost or world state; and a prefix copy cannot undo an action in a discarded suffix.
  We present an executable F# contract that separates facts from effect requests, makes scheduling explicit, and assesses a cut relative to projection, strict execution replay, external continuation, or a declared counterfactual-world observation. Preserved counterexamples show that general settlement is neither terminating nor confluent and that disjoint declared writes do not prevent read/trigger interference. Against 5,540 public runtime logs, all 317,296 projection cuts satisfy the stated observation, while 36,251 cuts split a model request and do not license continuation; another 120,969 are Conditional because a committed oracle result must be served from the record without re-execution. In 121 observed forks, 16,625 retained-prefix events have zero structural mismatches, but none crosses an external-effect boundary. A separate public offline conformance fork crosses a committed, recorded oracle boundary. Its generator observes that the inherited result is served without a second fixture-oracle call; its verifier checks receipt/log consistency and a fork-bound HMAC assertion under a public conformance key. The result reframes cheap forking as a property-indexed semantic contract with explicit evidence and environment preconditions.

title: A Novel BVH-accelerated Dynamic Ray-Tracing Channel Model for Vehicular Communication Systems
summary: Accurate and efficient channel modeling is critical for evaluating the sixth-generation (6G) networks, while dynamic ray-tracing (DRT) remains bottlenecked by its reliance on channel coherence time. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel bounding volume hierarchy-accelerated DRT (BVH-DRT), which introduces a mechanism shift from a time-driven update in DRT to a spatial-driven update. The proposed channel model clusters complex scatterers using the BVH method as pre-processing to establish a geometric coherence distance guided by transceiver kinematics, so that the ray update intervals in BVH-DRT can be autonomously adjusted to reduce the complexity. Furthermore, the non-stationary channel impulse responses are generated to evaluate delay-Doppler (DD) domain waveforms, including orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) and orthogonal delay-Doppler division multiplexing (ODDM). Validations in vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) scenarios demonstrate that BVH-DRT achieves spatial-temporal consistency with measurements and commercial software while significantly enhancing computational efficiency. Additionally, bit error rate (BER) evaluation highlights the severe impact of high-dynamic channels on waveform performance. The proposed framework is important for designing reliable communications and robust sensing in 6G networks.

title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions
comment: Total length is 42 pages including 3 tables (Table 1, Table 2a, Table 2b) and four figures. Tables and figures are at the end of the doucment
summary: Sample size calculations in two-arm clinical trials with survival endpoint often utilize the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. In case of nonproportional hazards (NPH), much research is ongoing with some newer methods developed that work well in specific scenarios. Recent developments have considered the nonparametric Max-Combo logrank test for both design and analysis of survival data with NPH. Although many approaches have been proposed for analyzing time-to-event data with NPH such as Restricted Mean Survival Time, Average Hazard Ratios, and piecewise exponential model with hazard ratios changing over time, translation into sample size calculation is not obvious and relies on simulations for very specific scenarios of NPH. In the parametric setting, accelerated failure time models that allow NPH but require a constant time ratio assumption (PT assumption) have been proposed. Recently, a parametric approach that simultaneously allows both nonproportional hazards (NPH) and nonproportional time (NPT) has been proposed. It utilizes the concept of Relative Time (RT) with two different Weibull distributions for the two trial arms in the case of monotonically increasing/decreasing time ratios. A key limitation is that the hypotheses leading to the sample size calculation rely on a single effect size defined at a specific survival percentile. In our current work, we extend the parent RT method by utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time (WRT) that allows us comparison of the full survival curves. Performance of the proposed method is compared to the Max-Combo method under different weighting schemes, and its operation characteristics are studied via simulations.

title: A Multi-Modal Robotic Framework for Physical GUI Interaction Testing
summary:
Automated testing of mobile applications remains challenging when realistic user interactions must be reproduced and GUI behavior verified without relying on invasive mechanisms such as instrumentation or ADB-level control. Existing approaches, including DLD and R-DLD, detect data loss triggered by activity restarts but still depend on system-level access, which limits their applicability on real devices.
  This doctoral research proposes RFNIT, a multi-modal, fully non-invasive robotic framework for physical GUI interaction testing on smartphones. RFNIT supports end-to-end automation by perceiving the device state through external sensing and executing physical interactions, enabling human-like actions while preserving reproducibility and execution accuracy.
  The framework integrates a vision-based perception module, an LLM-driven reasoning agent, and a robotic actuator capable of performing touch, swipe, and typing gestures. Multimodal data, including external camera images and OCR-extracted text, are combined to identify GUI elements and guide subsequent testing decisions.
  Preliminary results indicate that RFNIT accurately recognizes buttons, text fields, and virtual keyboards from external camera input, achieving over 85\% visual detection accuracy. Ongoing and future work will focus on improving robustness, repeatability, and coverage of GUI states during long-running testing sessions.

title: A Framework for Guaranteed Active Fault Diagnosis with Applications to Aircraft Systems
summary: Within the multiple-model framework, active fault diagnosis applies auxiliary control input signals to ex?cite the system such that fault modes are distinguishable. For aircraft systems, it has been pointed out by some rele?vant works that certain faults cannot be effectively detected and isolated in time without actively exciting the aircraft dynamics. However, existing works have not simultane?ously addressed the optimal auxiliary control design with theoretical guarantees and the FDI method with an effective mechanism for triggering the active fault diagnosis. Hence, we are motivated to propose a framework of active FDI for aircraft systems to explicitly address the aforementioned issue. Specifically, we first formulate a receding-horizon FDI scheme for estimating the likelihood of candidate fault modes with proved effectiveness, and then we propose a method for estimating mode probabilities, based on which a mechanism is designed for triggering auxiliary control for active fault diagnosis. The auxiliary control signal design is formulated such that the effectiveness for FDI is theoret?ically guaranteed and the disruption to nominal flight oper?ation is minimized. Numerical test results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: ShapleyOG: Fast Adaptive Shapley Value Estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes
summary: Shapley values are a central tool for attribution in machine learning. Since their exact computation requires evaluating the cooperative game to be explained on exponentially many player coalitions, they are typically estimated from a limited number of evaluations. Recently, ShaplEIG has shown that adaptively selecting the coalitions to evaluate substantially improves sample efficiency over classical estimators. This, however, comes at the cost of a sequential procedure that, in every iteration, refits a Gaussian process surrogate of the game and selects the coalition with the largest expected information gain about the Shapley values. The resulting computational overhead limits its applicability to costly games with low evaluation budgets. We present fast adaptive Shapley value estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes (ShapleyOG) to overcome this limitation. ShapleyOG leverages the fact that Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the game, and we show that under paired sampling a Gaussian process surrogate on this component alone yields the same Shapley value posterior and coalition selection criterion from half as many observations. Moreover, ShapleyOG refits the surrogate only on a sparse schedule and efficiently updates the selection criterion in between, and it extends quadrature-based computation schemes to the prior covariance of the Shapley values, which allows for exact or cheaper approximate computation. In extensive experiments on diverse games, ShapleyOG matches the estimation accuracy of ShaplEIG while reducing its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude. As a result, it outperforms state-of-the-art non-adaptive estimators at equal total computation time already when a single evaluation takes a tenth of a second and a budget of a few thousand evaluations suffices, thereby widening the regime in which adaptive coalition selection is applicable and pays off.

title: Beyond the Agent Harness: Boundary Criteria for Software-Factory Orchestration - A Single-Operator Case Study
comment: 37 pages, 3 figures. Ancillary files include E1 data, coding manuals, coded units, and analysis scripts
summary: Several recent systems add a layer above the coding-agent harness that organises many agent runs into continuous delivery. The existence of such a layer is not our contribution. What is missing is a rule for deciding which layer a mechanism or a failure belongs to. We propose boundary criteria based on an operational definition of a run. A mechanism confined to one run belongs to the agent harness. One that coordinates runs, hands state from one run to a later one, or is updated from run outcomes belongs to a factory harness. One that must change with the application domain belongs to the domain layer. Two residual tests assign infrastructure and model causes. For failures, we code where the defect originated, which control failed to stop it, and where it was fixed as three separate fields, and we require positive evidence before attributing a failure to the environment. We developed the criteria on documented failures from a single operator's pipeline serving six projects and on 26 components of three published systems. We then froze them and had two model coders of the same family apply them to the same descriptions of 46 held-out units. They agreed on all 26 mechanism layers and on 18-19 of 20 incident fields (kappa 0.86-0.93), but both coders recorded the incident as undetermined or unrecorded in 8-13 of the 20 cases per field, and each flagged half of all units as ambiguous, mostly for missing information. The check exposed conflicts in the rules; a revision that separates mechanism classification from incident attribution resolves them but, in a sensitivity re-coding, agreed less (kappa 0.78-0.93). Agreement here is neither accuracy nor usefulness, and human coders have not yet been tested. Case evidence and seven hypotheses are reported as preliminary.

title: Distributed Robust Model Predictive Control for Optimal Consensus of Unknown Multiagent Systems with Event-Triggered Communication
summary: In this paper, we study the optimal consensus problem for multiagent systems with unknown dynamics. We propose a robust model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes the control input and consensus sequences while enforcing state and input constraints. Within this framework, noisy offline data are used to construct nominal prediction models and quantify the associated uncertainty, which is explicitly incorporated into the robust MPC design. To solve the resulting optimization problem at each MPC update with reduced inter-agent communication, we develop a distributed gradient-projection alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm with an event-triggered information exchange mechanism and establish its convergence to the optimal solution. Furthermore, sufficient conditions are established to guarantee robust constraint satisfaction and practical consensus of the closed-loop multiagent system. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Task-Calibrated Random Features via Influence-Based Error Cancellation
summary: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, yet only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task. We propose Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balance frequency moments constructed from task-specific influence using weights shared across kernel entries. Closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration; the contribution is a reusable, task-derived calibration space. We show that first-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto this space. For kernel ridge regression, complete cancellation yields a non-Gaussian second-order limit. For kernel Stein discrepancy, a subset identity and disjoint-block variance decomposition eliminate the linear component of pilot noise. Positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation and support higher feasible calibration ranks. Paired experiments show improved approximation to exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets and to the exact empirical Stein discrepancy under a fixed alternative, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget. Gains are smaller with cross-validated ridge, landmark pilots require conservative rank selection, and near the Stein null allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.

title: How Python Audio Libraries Change Across Releases: Module Structure and Documentation
summary: Developers who upgrade a Python audio library need to know what changed in the code they import and whether the release notes say so. Release notes and breaking changes have been mined for general software, but the module structure of audio libraries and its documentation have not been studied together. We mine 56 audio repositories used in machine learning workflows: the import graph of 49 packages at 1,395 releases, joined to 20,864 release-note and changelog entries, labeled by three open-weight language models and checked against two human coders. We find that (1) the set of a package's top-level modules is unchanged in 86.1% of consecutive release pairs, while the set of module files is unchanged in 61.4%. (2) A major increment changes the top level 5.2 times as often as another increment, and major and 0.x minor increments together account for 48.7% of the observed changes. (3) When a release removes modules, its notes name 8.9% of the removal units under a lexical match, an estimated 4.3% after a hand check of the matches. (4) Longer notes are more likely to contain an entry labeled as structural, and within each length band this proportion is also higher for releases with module removals. We intend to release the aligned dataset and the pipeline

title: A Novel Asymmetric Distributed Voltage Regulation Scheme to Enhance the Utilization of Distributed Energy Resources
summary: Passive voltage regulation in distribution grids using distributed energy resources (DERs) is becoming the standard for feeder voltage management in both under-voltage and over-voltage scenarios. Their simple control, ease of implementation, and fast response make them ideal for distribution feeders with high-DER penetration. This paper proposes a novel distributed voltage control for DERs based on the voltage at the point of common coupling, inverter rating, and operating active power. The proposed control is designed to utilize feeder inverters efficiently to reduce the burden on the inverters in both under-voltage and over-voltage operations and increase the fairness in reactive power ($Q$) support in over-voltage operations. The proposed control is implemented in static and dynamic simulations of a real feeder to validate the performance. Results for the under-voltage scenario are also presented in the paper.

title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests for Conditional Tail Index Models
summary: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The tests are based on a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of estimating the null parameter. Within the conditional Hall class, we identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto approximation bias in the test process, permitting lower thresholds while preserving asymptotically correct size. We establish the validity of the tests via multiplier bootstrap. For log-linear models, bootstrap validity extends to settings in which covariates among observations above a common threshold concentrate and the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix tends to zero. We further propose a data-driven threshold selection rule based on an estimate of the Pareto approximation bias after projection. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.

title: When Does Combining Software-Effort Estimates Help? Evidence from Four Public Project Datasets
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Public aggregate results available on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23913209
summary: Combining estimates can reduce individual prediction errors, but an ensemble may also dilute an unusually accurate estimator or repeat errors shared by its members. We study these competing effects on four archival software-effort datasets (Kitchenham: 145 projects, Desharnais: 77, China: 499, Maxwell: 63) with 100 repeated 70/30 training and test partitions per dataset. Three conventional models (parametric regression, analogy, and random forest) are combined with each other and, in Kitchenham, with a recorded human estimate. Out-of-fold calibration errors drive five combination rules: equal weighting, inverse-MSE weighting, a nonnegative simplex combination, signed Bates-Granger weighting, and Bates-Granger with covariance shrinkage. All preprocessing is learned within training folds. Model-error correlations range from 0.54 to 0.97. In Kitchenham, the human estimate dominates: equal weighting raises mean test log-MAE from 0.239 to 0.455, a loss that remains significant under a corrected resampled t-test with Holm adjustment, whereas the simplex rule limits the increase to 0.250. In Desharnais, China, and Maxwell, every rule lowers mean log-MAE (by 1.3 to 8.6%) and BG with shrinkage beats the calibration-selected individual on 75, 83, and 83 of 100 splits, but none of these gains is statistically distinguishable from zero once the overlap between repeated splits is accounted for. On a completion-year split of Desharnais, equal weighting becomes slightly worse and inverse-MSE is near the individual baseline, while simplex and shrinkage retain mean gains of about 5%. Combining correlated effort estimates is therefore a conditional decision: the harm of naive pooling next to a dominant source is clear, while the benefit elsewhere is small and uncertain.

title: Truncated backpropagation through time induces a two-sided gradient turnpike property
summary: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the computational burden of training recurrent models by restricting gradient computations to shorter temporal contexts. This induces two distinct boundary effects: missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution, while truncating the backward recursion omits future information. This motivates decoupling the interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed. Under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians and mild regularity conditions, this leads to a two-sided gradient turnpike property: the error between truncated- and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with the distance from both context boundaries. We derive bounds for the averaged update gradient, yielding guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity; under unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, these further imply a bound on the resulting optimality gap. Numerical experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.

title: Clouded Representatives and Score Matching for Distributed Quantile Regression
summary: Quantile regression is widely used in high-stakes applications where the data are distributed across many sites and the individual records cannot be shared. The existing distributed methods for quantile regression typically require homogeneous sites, large sites, or synchronous communication, which are rarely all satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a new method named cloudqr. Each site summarizes its observations by a few Gaussian clouds, each given by the size, center, and covariance of a group of observations, such that the clouds match the score of the raw data exactly. A central server then fits the quantile regression on the clouds from all sites. We establish the convergence of cloudqr under mild conditions. With simulation studies and two real-world applications, we demonstrate the superior performance of cloudqr over the existing distributed methods.

title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
summary:
Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs. We study KG-AST, which scores each commit risk from git history and code-graph features before heavy tests or AI review run, so the budget goes to the riskiest commits first, and which hands the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. On 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model trained on other projects ranks commits so that heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49-64% of bug-introducing commits depending on the language, against 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the biggest change first.
  Every language beats the biggest-change baseline, by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4), and the model wins in 19 of the 20 projects. About twelve training projects suffice; richer features, tuning and cleaner labels did not help. An AI reviewer that sees only a commit's diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context), and about half of its findings that did not match a later fix were judged real by independent AI judges. A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding used in our retrieval work adds nothing measurable here: commit-risk AUC, bug review and severity ranking are unchanged or worse. The labels are noisy and the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers; no CI minutes were measured.

title: Safe Output-Regulation Flows for Constrained Optimization via Control Barrier Functions
summary: Control-theoretic approaches to constrained optimization have been widely studied by interpreting optimization algorithms as dynamical systems. This paper formulates constrained optimization as an output-regulation problem with state constraints, where equality-constraint residuals are treated as regulated outputs and inequality constraints as state constraints. Proportional--integral feedback is employed to drive the equality-constraint residuals asymptotically to zero, while a control barrier function (CBF) safety filter is used to ensure inequality safety throughout the optimization process. We establish feasibility of the CBF filtering program throughout the inequality-feasible set and local exponential convergence of the resulting flow. Under stronger global conditions, we further prove convergence from an entire connected component of the inequality-feasible set. Since exact implementation of the flow requires solving a CBF quadratic program at each state, we further develop a flow that approximates the CBF solution through multiplier updates. Moreover, we provide a unified formulation encompassing the two proposed flows and projected primal--dual dynamics. Numerical examples demonstrate convergence, safety, and computational tradeoffs of the proposed flows.

title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data
summary: Competitive balance shapes outcome uncertainty, fan interest, and league regulation, yet standard measures summarize realized standings and cannot separate structural ability differences from match-level randomness. We develop a Bayesian framework that infers structural competitive balance from longitudinal match outcomes. Team abilities are obtained by projecting Gaussian auxiliary variables onto a graph-fused l1 polytope whose radius measures total pairwise ability variation. The projection places positive probability on exact ties, so statistically indistinguishable teams form explicit rank tiers. The radius equals realized ability variation whenever the constraint binds, linking it to parity, detectability, and structural inequality. An adaptive finite-regime model lets competitive eras recur, emerge, and disappear while team hierarchies remain season specific. Simulations show accurate recovery of regimes, radii, abilities, and tiers. Applied to 25 English Premier League seasons, the model identifies a persistent shift to a more stratified league beginning in 2005/06, with 2010/11 the only later return to the compressed regime. It also shows that a close title race can coexist with wide league-wide separation and that head-to-head results can separate clubs level on points. The framework gives leagues a model-based measure of balance to inform debates on revenue sharing and financial regulation.

title: Boundary Projection Acceleration for 2D One-cell Inversions in the Scattering Limit
summary: Efficient radiation transport on modern high-performance computers requires algorithms that expose spatial parallelism while maintaining robust convergence. One-cell inversion (OCI) replaces the spatially sequential transport sweep of source iteration with a cell-local solve, making discrete ordinates transport space-parallel, but its spectral radius approaches unity in diffusive problems, and existing accelerators such as transport synthetic acceleration reintroduce sweeps. Here we show that projecting the OCI residual onto a low-order angular space on cell boundaries accelerates convergence in scattering-dominated problems without a transport sweep. We implement the projection in a two-dimensional simple-corner-balance discretization with two angular bases: a linear ($P_1$) basis and one augmented with a quadrant moment ($P_1Q$). Fourier analysis of an infinite homogeneous medium shows that both corrections reduce the spectral radius in optically thick, highly scattering regimes, with $P_{1}Q$ being most effective. Across several test problems, including a modified version of the void-duct streaming benchmark, the method accelerates diffusive and scattering cases but does not uniformly improve convergence in streaming dominated problems. We also find that $P_{1}Q$ is a more robust accelerator than $P_1$ in situations where the flux has strong angular variation. Boundary projection substantially improves OCI convergence in diffusive regimes, and these results delimit the regimes that require additional stabilization or richer projection spaces.

title: A Unified Multi-Encoder Framework for Music Lyric Intelligibility Assessment: Bridging Invasive and Non-Invasive Paradigms
summary: Lyric intelligibility significantly impacts music engagement and comprehension, especially for hearing-impaired individuals. Existing speech intelligibility metrics perform poorly in musical contexts due to differences in prosody, timing, and spectral dynamics. We propose a unified multi-encoder framework that supports both invasive and non-invasive modeling for robust lyric intelligibility prediction. By capturing complementary local acoustic-semantic alignments, global musical semantics, and ASR-derived textual cues, our method achieves superior performance over baselines on the ICASSP 2026 Cadenza dataset, with the best model achieving 26.61 RMSE, a $9.2$\% improvement over the baseline, demonstrating its flexibility and robustness.

title: A Partial-Matching Proof of the Neyman--Pearson Lemma
summary: Testing seeks to distinguish distributions, whereas matching seeks to identify their common mass. I show that this apparent opposition provides a direct proof of the Neyman--Pearson lemma. Maximal partial matching between the alternative distribution and a scaled null distribution separates them into a common component and two mutually singular residuals. An elementary dual problem then turns this separation into a testing rule: complementary slackness forces rejection on the alternative residual and non-rejection on the scaled-null residual, leaving freedom to randomize at the likelihood-ratio threshold. Thus the optimal test emerges from maximal matching rather than being proposed in advance. The matching profile also determines the optimal power envelope.

title: Recursively Testing and Vibe Debugging a Google AI Studio Generated Vibe-Coded Database Software Application
summary: This research paper proposes a broader definition of vibe coding, extending the original one with non-developers and natural languages other than English, and introduces the notion of vibe debugging, as well as a sound, complete, and optimal algorithmic methodology for testing and vibe debugging vibe-coded software applications. This methodology is illustrated by applying it to a vibe-coded real-world database application of medium complexity generated with Google AI Studio Pro. We prove that even non-developers can obtain a final bug-free and functional satisfactory application version, even in languages other than English. We also prove that, although Google AI Studio Pro has sophisticated built-in engines for both language analysis, software development, and automated testing, it is still making lot of mistakes, so testing and vibe debugging of its generated code is a must.

title: Simulation Modeling and Control of an Elastic Shaping Antagonistic Variable Stiffness Actuator
comment: 29 pages, 11 figures. Extends the structural study in arXiv:2609.18456 (ACIRS 2026) with dynamic modeling and closed-loop control evaluation
summary: Position--stiffness regulation of antagonistic variable stiffness actuators (VSAs) involves coupled nonlinear dynamics, parameter uncertainty, and feedback states that are not directly measured. This paper addresses this challenge through a simulation-based workflow that integrates elastic shaping, model verification, and layered nonlinear control. This study builds on a previously developed actuator comprising two crossed four-bar compliant transmission elastic units. Its optimized elastic mapping provides the structural basis, with an ADAMS torque-curve root mean square error (RMSE) of $2.57\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm}$ against the target. A control-oriented analytical model is implemented in Simulink and compared with the independently executed ADAMS model under matched inputs. The maximum joint-angle RMSE across the tested cases is $4.66\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}$. A layered controller combines extended Kalman filtering for state reconstruction, feedback linearization for nominal decoupling, and adaptive sliding-mode control for residual compensation. At the end of the nominal simulation, the joint-angle error is approximately $3.14\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad}$. The stiffness error is $3.07\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$ relative to a target of $50\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$. Parameter-variation and ablation tests assess tracking performance and the effects of the controller modules within the evaluated conditions. The resulting workflow links structural-response modeling, state estimation, and robust control assessment, supporting repeatable comparisons beyond nominal tracking alone.

title: A Unified Coordinate Descent Framework for Penalized Longitudinal Log-Contrast Quantile Regression
summary: Quantile regression characterizes heterogeneous covariate effects across the response distribution, but its extension to high-dimensional longitudinal compositional data poses substantial challenges, such as the nonsmooth check loss, the unit-sum structure of compositional covariates. Existing work is confined to Lasso penalization, and does not readily extend to nonconvex penalties. We propose CDaLCqr, a unified coordinate descent algorithm for penalized longitudinal log-contrast quantile regression accommodating popular penalties, such as adaptive Lasso, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD), and minimax concave penalty (MCP) within a single framework. The proposed method uses a Huber-type smooth approximation of the check loss and enforces the zero-sum constraint through an augmented Lagrangian formulation. CDaLCqr combines coordinate descent with majorization-minimization, yielding explicit updates through coordinate-wise quadratic surrogates. We show that the stopping tolerance controls errors in the zero-sum constraint and stationarity conditions. Under suitable conditions and sufficiently close initialization, we also prove local convergence of the coefficient and multiplier iterates, with an error bound decreasing by a fixed factor less than one each iteration. Simulations highlight the estimation advantages of SCAD and MCP variants and their sparse model identification. An application to Chinese provincial industrial data identifies interpretable, quantile-specific associations between sectoral composition and regional economic output.

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
comment: 10 pages, 3 tables. A shorter version of this work was published in the Proceedings of the Thirty-Fifth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-26), Demonstrations Track, pp. 8547-8550 (2026), doi:10.24963/ijcai.2026/1000. Includes code for the synthetic experiment
summary: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

title: Sharp Minimum-Rate Guarantees for Power-Based Discrete RIS Design
comment: in the submission process to WCL
summary: We characterise when desired-power optimisation guarantees the minimum user rate (MUR) in discrete reconfigurable intelligent surface systems with fixed precoding. For the weighted sum of desired powers, a bounded channel exists whose exact maximiser starves a user: no positive guarantee exists. For the minimum desired power, the retained fraction of the optimal MUR is at least a sharp constant set by the phase's power quality and residual interference. A semidefinite dual certifies it without enumerating phases. Minimum-power phases keep 88% of the optimum under weak reflection and about half under strong reflection; omitted interference causes most of the loss.

title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals
summary: We study distribution-free uncertainty quantification for a changepoint estimate in an offline setting. We observe a sequence with a single changepoint and are given an estimate of its location. The pre- and post-change segments are independent and each consists of i.i.d. (or, more generally, exchangeable) observations from arbitrary and unknown distributions. We introduce Changepoint LOcalization via Nested Exchangeability testing (CLONE), a novel method for constructing distribution-free confidence intervals around that estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centered at the reference estimate. Under these assumptions, CLONE provides finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator. Using a geometrically shrinking radius grid, CLONE requires only $O(log n)$ permutation tests. We characterize optimal scores for the framework and provide practical recommendations that result in sharp confidence intervals. Under mild assumptions, CLONE confidence intervals have asymptotically vanishing normalized length. Simulations and experiments on image and text data support our theoretical findings.

title: Certified folding-free deformable image registration: A whole-cell Jacobian certificate and a sequential variational solver
summary: Registration maps propagate labels, measure local volume change, and map results back through their inverses; requiring invertibility. Voxelwise checks can miss folds between grid points. We study the canonical continuous extension of a nodal displacement field by trilinear interpolation and give a test that proves its Jacobian determinant positive in every grid cell or rejects the map. The test is rigorous under IEEE 754 binary64 arithmetic (correct rounding, no contraction). With a fixed boundary, certification implies a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of the image domain. We introduce SeqVP, built around this certificate. A proximal Jacobian-determinant-curl formulation yields inner problems whose penalties on changes in the map, Jacobian determinant, and curl vanish to first order at the current iterate. The method decreases a fixed outer energy up to a floating-point resolution guard and certifies every committed iterate. After certified initialization, stopping at any time returns a folding-free map. A Poisson-preconditioned gradient method with Jacobian-aware step prediction and affine-scaling damping, initialized by certified handoff from an uncertified binary32 pre-optimizer, handles a 1 mm brain MRI with about 2e7 unknowns in 90 s on one GPU. On 49 held-out OASIS pairs, SeqVP achieves mean Dice 0.821 over 35 structures and 0.889 over 4 tissue classes, with certified zero folding. Gains are 0.022 and 0.025 over ANTs SyN, and 0.022 and 0.023 over uniGradICON with instance optimization at equal time (paired, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), but maps are rougher. SeqVP is level with ANTs on LPBA40, behind it on IBSR18, and ahead of all label-free baselines on 20 large-deformation pairs. On fields from nine methods, the certificate finds non-positive-Jacobian cells in every ANTs SyN map (median 10, missed by voxelwise checks) and in maps from NiftyReg, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, and TransMorph.

title: FUSEMOS: Perceptual Evaluation of Text-to-Music Generation with Dual-Encoder Fusion and Ranking-Aware Composite Loss
summary: Perceptual evaluation of generated music is essential for developing text-to-music (TTM) generation systems. Existing automatic music perceptual evaluation methods rely solely on the contrastive language audio pretraining (CLAP) model to extract both audio and text features for predicting human-annotated mean opinion scores (MOS), particularly for overall musical impression (OMI) and textual alignment (TA). However, CLAP is limited in capturing fine-grained musical attributes such as timbre and expressiveness \emph{etc}. To address this, we propose FUSEMOS, a dual-encoder fusion framework that integrates CLAP with MERT, a self-supervised model pretrained on large scale music audio, to better capture both high level semantic alignment and detailed musical characteristics for more accurate OMI and TA estimation. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of conventional regression losses in measuring human preferred relative ranking of music segments, we design a novel ranking-aware composite loss function. Experiments conducted on the MusicEval benchmark demonstrate that our approach outperforms the existing SOTA methods in both mean squared error and rank correlation metrics by a large margin.

title: Inference after selection on randomized p-values
summary: We consider inference on parameters and hypotheses selected using p-values. We provide a simple procedure to decompose a p-value into two components, one for inference and one for selection, that are independent under the null hypothesis. To control the Type 1 error rate conditional on selection of the null hypothesis from randomized p-values, we develop tests motivated by the selective inference approaches of data thinning, fission, and carving. Unlike the typical application of these approaches, however, our tests only make use of the p-values rather than the full data. Furthermore, we construct confidence intervals that attain the nominal conditional coverage and corresponding estimators. In the context of the file drawer problem, the winner's curse, and sequential testing, we show that our proposals offer both theoretical and empirical advantages over existing randomized and non-randomized approaches. Lastly, we apply our methods for selective inference on genetic associations using publicly-available p-values from the UK Biobank.

title: A Sharp Additive Bound for the Threshold Rule in Repeated Rent-or-Buy
summary: Motivated by context management in LLM agents, we study a repeated rent-or-buy model with schedule-independent history growth and a fixed reset price $K$, a discrete form of dynamic TCP acknowledgment: every call pays as rent the history accumulated since the last reset, and a reset clears it. The classical threshold rule is $2$-competitive, and no deterministic rule guarantees a smaller ratio. We show that, measured additively, its loss is governed by the changes in the growth: if the growth is constant on $P$ runs, the threshold rule, knowing neither the runs nor the horizon, pays at most $(2P-1)K$ more than the optimal schedule chosen with hindsight, and the coefficient $2P-1$ is sharp. If the growth is only within a factor $1+\varepsilon$ of $P$ runs, the bound holds up to a factor $1+\varepsilon$ and an extra $\varepsilon K$. The proof is a potential argument built from the relative value functions of the single-rate problems. On two runs no deterministic rule guarantees a loss below $2K$. A rule that also resets when the growth decreases guarantees $2K$, while the threshold rule can lose arbitrarily close to $3K$.

title: dynamicalnodes: Block Diagrams to ROS2 Graphs
summary: Here we introduce dynamicalnodes, a framework for rapid iterative prototyping of control and estimation algorithms within the Robot Operating System, or ROS. The framework leverages the theory of discrete-time dynamical systems to encode each component of a feedback system (e.g. reference generator, controller, plant, observer) as a pair of functions, denoted $(f,\,h) $, where $f$ is an evolution function and $h$ is an output function. With appropriate choice of domain and codomain, the $ (f,\,h) $ pairs can be composed to form feedback systems of arbitrary complexity. Moving from theory to practice, the user implements each $(f,\,h)$ pair in Python and encapsulates them in objects that facilitate composition and simulation. ROS executables are generated from these objects via rclpy, where relevant metadata such as network topology and publishing frequency are written automatically. The final result is a collection of rclpy files from which validated feedback systems can be spun up as live ROS graphs. We discuss the relevant theory behind the framework and then demonstrate the prototyping workflow applied to a canonical controls problem, a car with cruise control.

title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
summary: In this article, we study deep nonparametric regression trained via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects carefully calibrated Gaussian noise during optimization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks, we establish an excess-risk bound that simultaneously accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity, and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Under a Bernstein condition and within a stable SGLD regime, the excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the variance of injected noise, while the estimator retains the optimal rate for nonparametric regression under the Hölder smoothness condition up to logarithmic factors. This result provides an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal statistical perspective on the widely observed generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise. For per-sample clipped SGLD, we further establish an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic $μ$-GDP guarantee for the proposed estimator. We establish statistical convergence rates and differential privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained using SGLD, while explicitly accounting for both network approximation error and the effect of injected noise in the excess-risk bound. Extensive simulation studies and analyses of two real datasets examine the finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior of the proposed procedure.

title: Octopus: One Brain, Many Branches for Latent-KV Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Multi-agent LLM systems explore in parallel by spawning sub-agents with isolated context windows, whereas single-agent systems append every search and verification step into one growing trajectory. However, existing multi-agent frameworks duplicate prefix KV caches across branches, exchange findings by re-prefilling text summaries, and flatten or drop cross-branch dependencies during reinforcement learning (RL).
  We introduce Octopus, a single-model multi-agent RL framework in which all threads share one backbone and coordinate over a GPU-resident directed acyclic graph (DAG) of KV states through five primitives (fork, read_thread, wait_threads, rewind, commit). Octopus combines three co-designed mechanisms: (1) Zero-Copy Radix Forking, which spawns branches as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ cursor views over shared physical KV pages; (2) Attention-Only KV Mounting, which mounts a sibling thread's terminal KV blocks directly into full-attention layers while bypassing linear-recurrent states (Gated DeltaNet / Mamba-2), cutting off-task hijacking by $21\times$ ($57.9\% \to 2.7\%$) while retaining $92.2\%$ of full-text mutual information at zero extra KV allocation; and (3) a Packed DAG-GRPO Trainer, which packs all episode branches into one block-sparse attention pass and assigns counterfactual branch credit via leave-one-branch-out marginal rewards.
  Trained end-to-end with GRPO on Qwen3.5-4B over a sparse BM25 corpus, Octopus reaches $49.6\%$ accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus ($+17.5$ points over single-agent GRPO at 143K context and $+12.5$ points over text-summary multi-agent RL) and $51.2\%$ on OpenResearcher, outperforming dense-retrieval agents up to $250\times$ larger while increasing training throughput $3.3\times$ and cutting peak KV memory $2.8\times$.

title: When Does Inter-BS Interference Hurt Sensing in ISAC? An Exact Fisher Information Analysis under Finite-Alphabet Interference
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, submitted to IEEE possible publication
summary: In networked integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), a base station (BS) performing sensing using its own downlink signals is subject to interference from the downlink transmissions of neighboring BSs. This paper investigates the impact of the signal constellation and waveform on the sensing performance in the presence of such inter-BS interference. For any linear receiver, we show that the mean-squared cross-ambiguity between two random ISAC signals is invariant to the modulation bases and constellations. We then derive the exact Fisher information under finite-alphabet interference with a flat-fading link, which equals the interference-free Fisher information scaled by $1-γ\,\mmse_{\C}(γ)$, where $γ$ denotes the interference-to-noise ratio (INR) and $\mmse_{\C}$ is the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) in estimating an interfering data symbol from its noise-corrupted observation at the sensing receiver. Consequently, Gaussian interference is the worst case and corresponds to the CRB loss of the matched filtering, whereas finite-alphabet interference induces a non-monotonic CRB loss that peaks at intermediate INR and vanishes at high INR. The loss is waveform-independent for the flat-fading BS-BS link, and an expectation-maximization (EM) interference-cancellation receiver approaches the theoretical bound for delay estimation.

title: marp: Model-Averaged Inference for Parametric Renewal Processes in R
summary: Renewal processes model inter-event times between recurrent events using a parametric distribution, but selecting a single model can ignore model uncertainty and affect inference, particularly in small samples. This paper introduces marp, an R package for model-averaged inference in parametric renewal processes. The package fits six commonly used distributions, compares them using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, and reports selected-model and model-averaged estimates of the mean inter-event time, event probability and hazard function, with percentile and Studentised bootstrap confidence intervals. A simulation study under three data-generating models showed that model averaging did not improve point estimation but often improved interval coverage relative to the AIC-selected model. Applications to seizure-recurrence and engineering failure-time data illustrate the proposed methods. The marp package provides a reproducible framework for inference that accounts for model uncertainty in parametric renewal processes.

title: An Integrality-Gap Lower Bound of 1.2325 for Minimum Multiway Cut
summary: We prove that the integrality gap of the Călinescu-Karloff-Rabani relaxation for Minimum Multiway Cut is at least $1.2325$ when the number of terminals is large. By a result of Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008), it is therefore NP-hard, under the Unique Games Conjecture, to approximate Minimum Multiway Cut within a factor of $1.2325$. This improves the previously best known lower bound of $1.20016$ due to Bérczi, Chandrasekaran, Király, and Madan (2020).

title: Re-Planning Budgets under Admission Control in Grant-Free LEO Beam-Hopping Access
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, submitted to IEEE ICC 2027
summary: Reordering low-Earth-orbit (LEO) beam-hopping visits can reduce grant-free update delivery even when each region receives the same service time. We derive the largest limit on inter-frame position changes that meets a prescribed delivery-rate loss tolerance when every group is visited once per frame. The guarantee concerns a protected beam's spatially averaged long-run delivery rate relative to optimized periodic service under exogenous re-planning. Fixed admission can favor irregular visits, whereas admission optimized for each revisit interval makes the per-visit reward concave under sufficient conditions on transmission success. Periodic service is then optimal at a fixed mean interval. The shortest and longest allowed intervals determine the exact worst-case loss, attained by feasible alternating visit orders that respect every group's displacement limit. The resulting budget requires no estimate of the revisit-interval distribution and extends to independent stationary renewal updates. In a collision example with 40 groups and 40 resources per slot, increasing the loss tolerance from zero to 1% raises the limit from 17 to 24 positions. With independent priorities, the latter retains over 90% of the priority-weighted waiting-cost reduction achieved by unrestricted ordering. Received-power simulations under Rayleigh fading support the predicted loss.

title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget
summary: An experiment can be informative about the parameters of a working model and uninformative about whether that model is wrong. Adaptive design can reinforce this mismatch by repeatedly selecting settings where an incorrect model fits. We bound the power of any valid adequacy test in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, then distinguish information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model. It motivates a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed: the independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, but has no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG. A conditional futility bound explains why remaining time matters without proving the gate constant or its power. These results support separating parameter learning, model checking and detector performance; they do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.

title: Operationalizing Responsible AI in MLOps and ML Production: A Systematic Literature Review
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Systematic literature review of 44 primary studies
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled systems are increasingly deployed in operational environments where machine learning (ML) models interact with changing data, users, infrastructure, and organizational processes. While Responsible AI principles are widely discussed, less is known about how these principles are translated into concrete mechanisms within Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) and ML production workflows. This paper reports a systematic literature review of studies that operationalize Responsible AI in ML production. The review synthesizes evidence across monitoring and runtime assurance, audit and compliance, ML lifecycle integration, and traceability/provenance/documentation. Across the final study set, the literature shows a shift from abstract ethical principles toward engineering mechanisms such as drift monitoring, runtime checks, audit logs, provenance records, evidence bundles, governance gates, policy-as-code, model passports, and compliance-oriented documentation. However, the evidence base remains uneven: many studies propose architectures or prototypes, while fewer evaluate the mechanisms in realistic production settings, longitudinal operations, or organizational governance workflows. The review identifies a central gap around integrated, evidence-producing Responsible MLOps: current mechanisms often detect, document, or govern isolated parts of the ML lifecycle, but rarely connect runtime signals, ML lifecycle provenance, human accountability, and compliance evidence into closed operational loops. These findings motivate future software engineering research on traceable, evaluable, and operationally integrated Responsible AI support for ML production.

title: Auditory and Visual Virtualization in 6DoF XR: Effects on Plausibility and Dynamic Auditory Distance Perception
summary: Extended reality (XR) enables controlled yet naturalistic multisensory experiments, but its validity depends on whether virtualized cues are perceptually plausible and lead to behavior comparable to the real world. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to perceptually evaluate a six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) XR system that combines real-time room acoustic simulation, binaural rendering, and an audio-visually matched virtual replica of a large laboratory room in terms of both plausibility and behavior. In two experiments with 45 participants, we investigated how auditory and visual virtualization affect plausibility and dynamic auditory distance perception (ADP). A plausibility experiment compared real and virtual sound sources in audio-augmented reality (AAR) and virtual reality (VR), while a locomotion-based ADP experiment assessed distance-judgment accuracy, signed error, and task effort across four virtualization conditions. The system produced plausible binaural rendering in both AAR and VR, with higher plausibility in VR, indicating that perceptual requirements for XR audio depend on the visual reference frame. In the ADP task, any form of virtualization reduced accuracy and increased effort, although performance remained high overall. Virtual audio produced a bias toward nearer perceived source distances, whereas visual-only virtualization reduced accuracy without a significant directional bias. These effects did not add up in full VR. Overall, the findings demonstrate the strong potential of current 6DoF XR systems for interactive perceptual research, while revealing that task-specific behavioral validation may be necessary.

title: Identification and Bounding of Joint Expectation over Potential Outcomes
summary: The joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes $(Y_1,Y_0)$ is a fundamental quantity in causal inference, particularly when investigating the variation or heterogeneity of causal effects. This paper provides novel assumptions for their identification: comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity. These assumptions offer a unified framework for their identification across discrete, continuous, and mixed outcome variables. In the absence of these assumptions, we derive sharp bounds for two broad classes of functions, yielding new results for bounding moments of individual causal effects, which are central to measuring effect heterogeneity. We present corresponding estimation methods and illustrate them in simulation studies and real-world datasets.

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
summary: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

title: A Conformal Transmit-Reflect Array Enabling Multifunctional Bidirectional Beam Switching for Emergency Communication System
summary: This article presents a conformal transmit-reflect array (CTRA) that enables bidirectional multibeam switching through a single metasurface aperture for emergency communication applications. To realize reconfigurable bidirectional beam switching, a transmit-reflect integrated element (TRIE) is developed by combining a polarization-selective transmissive structure with a complementary-symmetric reflective structure. The proposed element enables independent control of the cross-polarized transmission and reflection phases while exhibiting stable performance under oblique incidence. To support practical conformal implementations, a geometrical-optics-based phase compensation method is applied to cylindrical geometries, enabling effective wavefront control across the conformal aperture. By incorporating a polarization-switchable feed array (PSFA), multifunctional beam switching is achieved in the forward, backward, and bidirectional operating modes. The PSFA is configured as a nonuniform curved linear array near the focal region, enabling feed-selective beam switching within $\pm 30^\circ$ in both the $+z$ and $-z$ directions through selective excitation of the corresponding feed elements. The full-wave simulation results agree well with the measurements. The proposed CTRA achieves peak gains of 24.1 and 24.8 dBi in the forward and backward modes, respectively. The maximum aperture efficiencies in the forward and backward operating states are 28.4$\%$ and 33.4$\%$. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed CTRA, making it a promising candidate for adaptive emergency communication systems.

title: Sequential Certification of Partially Identified Product Targets: Information Limits and Adaptive Sampling
summary: We study the cost of certifying a scalar target driven by a product of centered Bernoulli means when an unobserved terminal gate leaves irreducible uncertainty. Each factor can be queried independently at a price. We derive the exact identified interval and determine when a requested accuracy is feasible. At every fixed strictly feasible interior instance, the optimal high-confidence expected cost is $(1+o(1))\log(1/δ)/D^*$, where $D^*$ is an answer-and-allocation information game; a globally honest procedure attains this benchmark. At product cancellation, we solve the game through a one-dimensional inverse-KL equation and explicit cost weights. For two tickets, quartic projections and rational bounds give checkable global optimality gaps. Joint confidence--precision limits expose a failure of the analyzed fixed pilot: it can cost asymptotically at least twice the optimum. A charged, precision-aware pilot with checkpoint certification restores optimal expected cost in exact arithmetic when $\log\{e+\log(1/g)\}=o(\log(1/δ))$ for effective precision $g$, including exponential and certain double-exponential precision scales. Pooled rescue preserves validity and cannot increase observation cost on coupled paths. Implemented auditors verify returns by rational inequalities; reproducible experiments show both savings and finite-confidence overhead. These guarantees concern the specified independent-reference model and its scalar target.

title: When Can Self-Play Fix a False Belief? Answer Keys, Pass Bands and Replacement Rules in an Execution-Grounded Loop
summary: Self-play loops in which a model writes tasks, derives an answer key and trains on its own matching solutions are often called grounded when the key comes from executing code. We ask which false beliefs such a loop removes. We run expert-iteration self-play with Qwen3-4B-Base on output-prediction tasks, vary the source of the answer key, and track natural beliefs about Python semantics and two misreadings of task specifications planted by fine-tuning ("at most n" read as < n; "the k-th smallest" read as 0-indexed). Executing the generator's own code gave a key that encoded the "at most" misreading on every audited task, and training on it never raised the truth rate above 0.03. A key from an implementation by the unplanted model, a teacher without the error, raised it to 0.23-0.58 after three rounds in four runs. A correct key is not sufficient: the pass band, which keeps tasks solved 1-7 times of 8, admits almost no corrective task while a belief is held on nearly every sample. Execution keys sharply reduced both natural runtime beliefs on diagnostic items in both seeds. Corrections came with replacement rules that fail on neighbouring items the old belief got right. The robust case, present in all four spec runs, is that after the "at most" fix the model increasingly counts the nearest value above a limit that is absent from the list (overcount 0.18-0.38 of control samples at round 3), a case our planted generators almost never wrote (4 of 10,924 tasks); diagnostic-only metrics miss it. Asked for those cases, the planted generator wrote none in 2,061 checkable tasks, against 27% for the untrained unplanted model in one round. Both generators often moved the request into the specification instead ("the cap itself does not count"), and a decorrelated key follows the specification.

title: Joint Flexible Beamforming, Resource Allocation, and Task Buffering for Movable-Antenna Enabled MEC Systems
summary: The proliferation of computation-intensive applications, such as generative artificial intelligence and low-altitude economy services, demands mobile edge computing (MEC) systems that are both energy-efficient and adaptable to highly dynamic workloads. However, conventional MEC architectures rely on fixed-position antennas with limited spatial flexibility and rigid single-slot task execution models, which fail to accommodate bursty traffic and time-varying channels. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel MEC framework empowered by movable antennas (MAs) and task buffering. Unlike traditional approaches, our system enables continuous antenna repositioning to maximize array gains and decouples task generation from immediate execution via buffer queues, allowing for flexible multi-slot scheduling. We formulate a stochastic optimization problem to minimize long-term energy consumption by jointly optimizing receive beamforming, MA positions, and computing resources. Leveraging Lyapunov optimization, we transform the long-term problem into tractable per-slot subproblems and develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms the benchmark schemes in terms of energy consumption, while maintaining stable task queues under unpredictable traffic conditions.

title: Bayesian Spatio-temporal Modeling of Multi-Site Wastewater Surveillance Data
summary: Wastewater surveillance provides population-level evidence of infectious disease activity.
